rationale: The cannabinoid arm had at least one fall in 4 of 31 participants versus 3 of 30 on placebo. Both formulations contained strawberry extract and neither assigned raw fruit. The count is people with a fall, with no recurrent-event rate or strawberry estimate.
The strawberry-containing group pools seven fruits and has adjusted HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.03) per 20 g/day for fall-related admissions. No separate fruit, Parkinson stratum or total fall count.

Six fruits were assigned together. The primary relevant reported postural sway comparison was inconclusive (time by phase p=.457). The 2021 registration and the article describe the same crossover. No strawberry-only or falls contrast.

Gait speed improved with the nutrient formula compared to maltodextrin. Strawberry and vanilla flavors were available in both arms. The 140-person registration and 127-person outcome analysis describe one trial, with no fall-frequency result by flavor.

Freeze-dried whole strawberry and placebo showed no group effect on fear of falling (p=.518). The entry screen excluded recent fallers. Gait, balance and fear differ from observed fall frequency. The erratum reports the same cohort.

The registered 47-person trial chose gait speed and excluded recent unexplained falls. The likely companion USDA project records do not add an independent result. Registry and project reports provide no outcome.

The current registry and original protocol describe the same isolated-fisetin trial after breast cancer chemotherapy. A fall question is planned alongside gait distance. No outcome results have posted.
The prevention cohort showed a tissue dopamine response but no reported strawberry improvement in the Figure 5 water-maze contrasts. Extract diet, experimental aging and no spontaneous fall measure.

This distinct reversal cohort assigned strawberry extract in older rats. Only blueberry showed improvement on reported rod-walk and rotarod comparisons. Strawberry neurochemical findings cannot supply a fall sign.
Author abstract reports no reversal of aged-mouse motor-test deficits. Arm-level results remain open. This species and design are distinct from the two rat studies. No raw fruit or clinical falls.

High-dose leaf extract prolonged mouse rotarod latency and shortened pole turning. The reported cell-line experiment overlaps the poster. Leaves and test performance provide no transferable raw fruit and spontaneous fall direction.
A strawberry odor item showed nominal group discrimination and did not enter the final three-item panel. The grouping is freezing status. The study does not compare eaten fruit or falls.

Adequate combined produce corresponds to lower adjusted odds of previously reported injurious falls. The female and male estimates differ materially. The pooled exposure, recall and absence of a Parkinson stratum leave no strawberry effect.
Daily fruit and vegetable consumption is associated with lower adjusted odds of prior-year falls (OR 0.55). No strawberry identity, separate fruit estimate or Parkinson population.
Case-control dietary comparisons use aggregate fruit frequency, with cases defined by fractures after falls. There is no species-specific or recurring Parkinson fall contrast.
Seasonal strawberry consumption is observed in the underlying diet and microbiota cohort. Diet is measured rather than assigned and no fruit-only or fall outcome is reported.

reporter: assessment authors citing a regional adaptation report
rationale: Wild strawberries appear as traditional First Foods. The source documents food use and access without reporting a symptom outcome or first-person efficacy observation.

The later poster reports 38.53 versus 23.58 autoshaping trials per 60 minutes with milkshake versus peanut oil. The 13-animal milkshake group likely overlaps the ASN poster and exact cohort lineage remains unverified. This result concerns engagement, with distinct food formulations and no fall endpoint.
All applicable task groups receive the same milkshake reward. The original paper measures cue approaches and related neural signaling and provides no comparative strawberry or fall outcome.

The food-related dermatology entries discuss strawberry alongside other possible reaction triggers. The definitions provide no inspectable fruit-specific outcome comparison or fall frequency. Descriptive clinical terms are separate.

P-557 and the fuller published article share the three fruit extracts and investigators. Relative membrane findings depend on the measured property and model. These are applied extracts in laboratory tests with no mobility result.

The linked P-603 and authors' paper use strawberry leaf extracts in red-cell or model-membrane assays. Exact sample overlap is uncertain. A cell or model result supplies no oral fruit fall comparison.

Two or more weekly strawberry servings versus less than one favored the adjusted cognitive slope by 0.03 standard units (95% CI 0.00 to 0.06). Preparation, fall counts and Parkinson-specific estimates are unavailable.
The laboratory preparation comparison studies four other wild berries. The strawberry details trace to separate animal and human references rather than these assays.

The older-adult survey reports strawberry-flavored supplement preference. The falls findings printed on the same page are from a separate vitamin D analysis. There is no assignment or falls estimate for the strawberry exposure.

The grouped strawberry, cherry and grape report compares overeating-related responses by food-addiction status. Preparation and individual fruit are unresolved. No fall outcome or Parkinson population is reported.

Early operant performance in irradiated rats favored a 2% strawberry extract diet. Later comparisons did not separate and irradiated controls were depleted. The assay records bar presses and cannot estimate Parkinson falls.

The separate 1.5 Gy operant experiment reports no difference at six months and a favorable strawberry extract comparison at twelve months. Full figures remain open. The assay is not a fall-frequency proxy.

Drug-induced learned taste avoidance in irradiated rats favored both berry diets in the amphetamine condition, with no reported change in the lithium condition. Cohort linkage with the later same-dose operant work is unverified.

The recovered original compares three oil-based diet periods using processed drinks and margarine. LDL was 0.17 mmol/L higher than the oleic period. Two participants reported transient GI discomfort. Pressing method and resting tremor were not reported.

Poison-center reports include tremor and weakness after whole kernels. The same investigator observed no tremor in four experimentally exposed dogs. The overlapping series and trial are one lineage. Neither studied expressed oil, resting phenotype or Parkinson disease.

Thirteen Australian field cases described hindlimb weakness, recumbency and pain after reported raw or roasted kernels. The case series differs from the US poison-center lineage. It supplies no separate rest-tremor outcome.
Pure macadamia-oil application did not significantly change skin flare or erythema in the author abstract. The comparison involved skin application and no tremor assessment.
The published conservation consultation records traditional uses of the kernels for food and trade. No pressed oil preparation, symptom or comparative response is described.

The dissertation reports the registered oil-blend comparison. Eight people entered the macadamia arm and seven contributed interpretable hydrogen transit. The groups did not differ significantly in transit response. No movement outcome or pressing grade.

Seventeen participants per family-history group ate the same macadamia-oil meal. Postmeal metabolic responses did not significantly differ across groups. Pressing grade and tremor were unreported, and no oil-free comparator was included.

The distinct BRAVO comparison enrolled 125 and stopped early. It used macadamia-oil placebo against omega-3 and planned affect and cognitive assessments. The official registry has no posted results or Parkinson tremor outcome.

Protocol compares macadamia and coconut oils in a skin-absorption and metabolic context. Target enrollment was 16. Results and actual participant counts are absent from the official record. No food intake or tremor measure.

555 were randomized and 245 completed. Cognition, mood and resilience did not show clear group-by-time effects. The 2019 protocol, 2021 outcomes and later trainee analysis share a cohort. No untreated arm, pressing grade or rest observation is established.

One person reported less numbness and tingling after unrefined oil. A copied version and serving clarification duplicate the report. The record supplies no diagnosed Parkinson disease, movement endpoint or verified cold pressing.

The paper and reports describe two crossover samples of 16 and eight healthy students with separate figures. Acute alertness and fatigue contrasts do not estimate tremor. Outcome reports and the registry belong to the same family, and grade is unreported.

The abstract reports cerebellar staining and oxidative or inflammatory biomarker changes in a potassium-dichromate rat model. Full dosing, pressing grade and denominators remain unverified. The accessible text gives no interpretable motor or tremor result.

The Methods specify room-temperature hydraulic pressing. Comparative physicochemical and fatty-acid results establish process differences. The body and abstract attribute one percentage to different comparators. No participant or motor measure.

Eight of eleven historical Parkinsonian cases had tremor. Injected drug in oil and wax and oral belladonna lowered amplitude without materially changing incidence or rate. No oil-only exposure. The 1951 Ebin review is the same study family.

The 200-person clinical series covered several diagnoses. The author describes possible relief of painful rigidity with the injected drug and gives no individual tremor estimate or oil-only comparison.
Three of six animals received the drug dissolved in injected peanut oil. The reported effect is on levodopa-induced dyskinesia. Rest tremor appears in model description without an oil-only contrast.

Both diets contained peanut oil. The low rod yielded longer retention under the low-alpha-linolenic acid diet, the high rod and traction comparisons were inconclusive or unchanged, and some learning measures were weaker. No resting-tremor assessment.
The peanut-plus-rapeseed blend was the comparison for salmon-palm oil, with several dietary fatty acids changing. The fish-oil blend reduced general activity or changed habituation.

Six of sixty participants with peanut allergy reported reactions after crude oil, including two observable or measurable reactions. None reacted after the refined oil. Outcomes are acute allergy signs, with no identifiable rest-tremor response.

One trial assigned 129 healthy adults to eight weeks of peanut, olive, safflower oil or no study oil. The analyzed denominator for the activity result is unverified. Its companion paper reports no significant change in general activity, and neither report assessed tremor.
Measured fatty acids, tocopherols and phytosterols in specified cold-pressed oil. Availability of measured composition supplies no observed symptom contrast.
The table associates peanut-oil massage with infantile paralysis. This row identifies no direct witness, measured response or comparable oral route.
Table 2 records customary cooking and topical uses. Study citation counts measure use reports and cannot establish response or clinical effect.
The combined methanolic almond, peanut and watermelon seed extract favored less block catalepsy and greater activity. It did not test peanut oil, an isolated seed arm or a resting-tremor outcome.

The main report identifies oil-based control spread in healthy adults and tests cognition, stress and mood. Registration and later companion outcomes belong to the same intervention. No distinct oil-free comparator or tremor endpoint.

The ENHANce trial and nested TEMPUS-FUGIT use a peanut-oil omega-3 placebo in older adults with sarcopenia. The protocol and feasibility report address physical function, and the family has no separate Parkinson tremor result.
Metformin-treated outpatients consumed dietary oils including groundnut. The reported glucose and lipid outcomes do not record tremor or an acute hypoglycemic movement phenotype.
Shared diet in 16 patients includes cantaloupe. Supplement S2 and body Figure 4 score composite motor change. No fruit-level contrast, preparation or separate tremor estimate.
Same cohort as PMID23661325. Adjusted occurrence RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.72–1.38) combines four cucurbits. The indication is diagnosis occurrence and there is no separate raw-fruit comparison.
GliSODin favored memory in the restraint stress experiment. The supplemented mice were assessed for spatial learning and tissue endpoints.
A ripe pickling-melon versus muskmelon juice contrast concerns glycemia in people with diabetes. Neither a resting-tremor nor isolated raw flesh effect was reported.
Table 5 has a dose- and time-dependent pattern of rotarod means. Methods describe falls and the table gives time. Table 1 describes general behavior depression with no tremor item.
Table 3 gives shorter rotarod retention and Table 4 higher actophotometer activity. The abstract characterizes the rotarod as improved. The exposure is rind extract.
Crossover exposes volunteers to servings of separate unripe melon landraces or cucumber. Measured appetite and food reward without a tremor assessment.
The separate survey describes food experiences. Participant overlap with the crossover is unverified and its published outcomes do not inform rest tremor.

Mahlouji lists historical tremor and melon together only at the review level in separate tables. The Dadmehr textual analysis concerns a broader condition. Shared textual sources are plausible and no independent first-person response is established.
Rock melon is a named exposure in a registered crossover. Planned outcomes are glycemic index and load, and as of the review no results were available.
The capsule protocol lists frailty and quality-of-life outcomes. Registry results are absent and a named raw-fruit or resting-tremor comparison is not planned.
In mobility-limited older women, motor and fatigue differences are inconclusive. Capsules contain a Vauclusien melon extract and wheat gliadin.
Healthy men trained during a human supplement trial. The dried melon concentrate comparison did not give a clear between-group physical-fatigue difference or a separate tremor outcome.
A 61-participant healthy-adult comparison registered as NCT01767922 reports stress and fatigue. The proprietary freeze-dried concentrate and its endpoints cannot inform the frozen tremor outcome.

Regulatory review records tremor at the highest essential-oil toxicity exposure. The original case protocol and identity of the 2000 pamphlet animals remain open. Acute intoxication and toasted-fruit intake differ.
Oral methanolic fruit extract shortened experimenter-imposed bar posture. The assay did not score tremor.
Fresh leaf oil changed open-field and maze behavior in healthy mice. Separate five-animal limit screen disclosed no overt toxicity and gave no tremor count.

Oil group III shortened the bar posture relative to reserpine-only group II descriptively. Group IV was levodopa/carbidopa. Figures do not annotate the oil versus model comparison, and there was no item-level tremor.
Roasting changed the volatile profile, including lower fennel estragole. Full time, heat and sample-specific composition are open. No biological outcome was tested.
Cultivated and wild accessions differ greatly in starting volatiles, with a separate quantitative estragole estimate. The study has no roasting condition or symptom outcomes.
Whole crushed seed pellets lowered home-cage crossings and increased open-field center crossings. Toasting and resting tremor were outside the experiment.

The acute Table 1 records no convulsions or tremors in either fenchone or vehicle group. Methods and later table sample counts differ. The isolated compound comparison leaves the culinary Parkinson direction open.
A different methanolic extract had no reported deaths and no separately reported tremor outcome in the author abstract.
Boiled leaves and a separate claim about the fruit are documented under broad falij use. No firsthand fennel rest-tremor outcome or Parkinson diagnosis is identified.
Generalized seizure followed exposure to an unknown amount of fennel essential oil in cake in a person with epilepsy. No frozen outcome was recorded.
Repeated injections of leaf-and-stem juice were associated with convulsions. Route and dose units vary in the paper. No tremor outcome matches the claim.
Anethole given before rotenone improved rotarod and selected stride results. Resting tremor appears in the introduction as a disease feature.
Concentrated fruit extract reduced rotarod retention and grip in healthy mice. This does not identify a tremor phenotype.
Peri-lesion oral methanol extract favored coordination and grasp. Post-lesion-only comparisons were inconclusive. Neither was a tremor measurement.
Conference abstract gives rotarod, open-field and passive-avoidance results. Extract dosing and specific effect sizes remain open. The 2024 paper tests a separate in vivo challenge.
Oral fruit extract under LPS improved late coordination with no clear early result. No tremor assessment exists in the studied outcome set.
Tremors followed contaminated produce in cattle. Nitrate was measured in green and white plant waste and ruminal contents. No toasted seed or Parkinson exposure was isolated.
Fennel was held in a bundled seasoning oil during frying comparisons. The study measures aroma and composition without a separate fennel contrast.
The February conference abstract reports a concentration change in five people; the November Figure 4 lacks a plotted denominator. Treat the reports and Nomoto citation as one family for this review.
The clinical pilot assessed the separate rest item under cabergoline. No fruit was compared or measured.

Three people had lower UPDRS after antibiotic addition, with qualitative improvement in rest tremor or rigidity. Four were unchanged. The report gives no separated values for the item and the exposure is a different inhibitor.
The authors describe general motor improvements after itraconazole addition. One concentration and no separately reported resting-tremor change.
Whole fruit components and juice affected felodipine in a crossover. The food matrix effect cannot establish a comparable effect on cabergoline or symptoms.
Fresh white pulp changed measured exposure in healthy volunteers taking different calcium antagonists. No Parkinson drug or outcome was tested.
Grapefruit was listed in the mixed menu eaten by both Parkinson groups. No isolated ingredient or separate rest result.
The delay and severity description refer to an aggregate of induced signs. Timing of acute rat signs cannot specify resting-tremor severity.

Mean induced seizure tremor onset delayed in the drug-plus-juice arm versus drug plus water. The tested table comparator is the challenge-only arm. The stated denominator refers to the two beverage arms with nine rats each.
The registry concerns aroma and immediate brain signals or subjective responses. It gives no posted results.
The flavored drink observation does not describe a resting-tremor change. Regular grapefruit consumption, and added-sugar tremor, are different reports.
Injected isolated naringin and tissue degeneration in a rat model. No separate symptom sign.
The pretreatment and post-lesion comparisons separate tissue preservation from restoration in mice. No symptom measure.
Oral isolated limonin and general motor activity, with the exact task outcome requiring full methods.
The original isolated injection changed rod and pole behavior. Those tasks assess other motor functions, without a resting-tremor score.
The ground-soybean adjunct comparison gives longer ON and less dyskinesia. The abstract does not separate resting tremor or compare refined oil.
Spirography improved after both active octanol formulations. The pooled adverse-tremor and inconsistent six-hour results cannot isolate soybean oil.
Only the drug comparator varies against a shared oil vehicle. The prespecified essential postural tremor timepoint was inconclusive and later signals favor the drug.
Acoustic voice measures favored the active drug over the soybean-oil placebo. No oil-free placebo identifies a soybean oil effect and the refining grade is unspecified.

At day seven, 2.1 versus 4.7 (estimates read from Figure 4a) in highest oral whole-plant methanol-extract versus vehicle groups, eight mice per group. Fresh petioles carry identified extract compounds. Their effective dose and mediation in the mouse trial are unresolved.
The fresh petiole analysis found apigenin and luteolin also measured in the experimental extract. Chemistry supports an exposure link and supplies no independent symptom result.

Pharmaceutical butylphthalide compared off-medication tremor pooled across three types. The purported composite exceeds the stated maximum and nearly reproduces a quality-of-life row. The separate rest result cannot be interpreted.
One public contributor reported previous tremor, uncertain diagnosis and general benefit with seed extract, coffee and mannitol. No tremor change was attributed to a single exposure.

Two prints of one cohort's turkey frequency versus pooled self-reported tremor graphic. The tile is extremely close to zero on the positive side. Cooking, separate rest item, adjusted estimate, uncertainty and analyzed denominator are unverified.

Tremor returns in qualitative Figure 2 and 3 timelines after protein challenge in two participants. The third revised-load participant has no figure and the lower-load comparison has a different protocol. The authors give no specific rest score or baked exposure.

Five participants reported worsening general symptoms on an 80 g protein breakfast. Three also reported dyskinesia or restlessness with the high-carbohydrate meal. The balanced meal favored pegboard performance. No individual rest result or food ingredient is reported.

The author abstract separates a shorter response under the unusually high protein formula from inconclusive usual-allowance comparisons. There is no separate observed tremor subtype or comparable food preparation.

The Parkinson group showed supine hypotension and worsening of an aggregate motor score after a shared liquid meal. The twenty denominator refers to the Parkinson group rather than the sixteen controls.
Postprandial OFF time was shorter during the assigned low-protein product diet. The comparison supplies no separate rest measurement and cannot estimate an isolated baked-turkey effect.

An independently identifiable anecdote describes worse perceived medication effect during one holiday with repeated leftover turkey. Stronger attribution would require timing or food controls and a separately observed symptom. The quoted question counts as no additional observed event.

Six diet-alone participants and ten assigned the same fig-containing diet plus bowel cleansing. Preparation and individual consumption are missing. Motor totals, including Figure S2, do not provide a separate resting-tremor contrast.

A concentrated fruit extract reportedly favored general motor measures in haloperidol-treated rats. The available author abstract gives no item-level rest tremor estimate or active-exposure bridge to raw fruit. Keep full methods open.

Methods identify two bark formulations in 18 rats at assignment. Tables 11–13 are biochemical and have unclear analysis denominators. Discussion of a fruit-extract catalepsy result does not establish that arm in the experiment.
Groups of six per test received an aerial-part extract. Alertness and spontaneous activity fell, and rotarod time shortened. The assays lack a Parkinson or resting-tremor outcome.

A modern review lists Anjir and phenolic compounds as a potential Parkinson-related plant. Reference 20 leads toward fruit chemistry with bibliographic inconsistencies. No firsthand remedy or symptom outcome is available.

Three fresh fig cultivars had measured phenolics. The chemistry connects the traditional review's candidate reference to raw fruit, while there is no measured mediator match to the rat experiment or efficacy outcome.

Table 3 gives 3/40 tremor events for commercial fig-and-almond syrup versus 0/40 in each other arm. The active comparison changes other formulation components, all children took methylphenidate, case definition and baseline severity are absent, and events are sparse. This is a formulation safety observation without a transferable sign for raw fig and Parkinson rest tremor.

Homogenized fresh fig fruit provides preparation context. The hypoxia study measures Y-maze behavior and biochemistry. The reported total and listed group counts differ; no rest tremor comparison was reported.

The comparison exposed plasma from four Parkinson donors and one control to extract of fig male flower buds. Replicate enzyme assays do not observe the participants' tremor or an effect of edible fig.

Two copies of one graphic for the same cohort give a small inverse tile for unspecified olive oil and pooled self-reported tremor. There is no pairwise estimate, uncertainty, grade or separate rest item. The 2017 composite symptom analysis overlaps and has no separate tremor result.
Exact oil grade administered by injection improved rotarod and activity under toxin exposure. An acute tremor observation was outside the comparative endpoints.
The ketogenic recipes use extra-virgin olive oil. During the early phase, 12/24 versus 3/23 reported worsened tremor or rigidity. This is a bundled diet comparison with a combined adverse endpoint.
The oil association addresses Parkinson case status, with no within-disease separate tremor estimate or confirmed grade.

Table 2 shows one attenuation in ten tremor reports and prose mentions transient worsening without a count. The study selected volunteers; preliminary report overlap and separate rest outcomes remain open.
Named authors describe mustard among pungent dietary items and propose a general link to shaking. There is no firsthand treatment response.
Appendix A lists mustard within a menu. No ingredient comparison or separate rest result is reported.
Registered total scale and related white-seed enzyme formulation trail. Clinical use of the exact formulation and outcomes remain unverified.
An isolated compound with a registered total motor scale, unknown overall status and no posted results. There is no culinary-comparator premise.
Unheated brown powder added to cooked broccoli changes urinary metabolite recovery in healthy adults.
Measured raw and roasted black seed chemistry. Total glucosinolates fell. Preexisting isothiocyanate results were inconclusive.
Original bar, grip and coordination figures assess leaf extract. No rest-tremor rating or culinary seed comparison.
Relative glucosinolate signals declined after roasting. No measured Parkinson symptom or preparation-equivalent human dose.
The processed mustard adjunct raises measured urinary sulforaphane metabolite recovery. The study has no human Parkinson or rest-tremor outcome.

Sixty-one people randomized to isolated caffeine or placebo. UPDRS III rest tremor differed by -0.32 (95% CI -0.73 to 0.10) and -0.28 (-0.83 to 0.27) at weeks three and six. Both timepoints use the same trial. Tea chemistry confirms caffeine in the beverage with substantially smaller amounts per reported serving.

A caffeine dose escalation without an external comparator gives a within-group rest score reduction of 1.18 points at two weeks. Tremor worsening and physiological tremor occurred among discontinuation reasons. Twenty-five participants described, with substantial attrition.

Six percent of survey respondents with Parkinson perceived worse tremor with coffee. The same publication reports no clear increase after acute caffeine and does not give a separate compatible rest estimate. Group linkage and timing are unresolved, so no additional family count was assigned.

Brewed black tea averaged about 39 mg caffeine per 200 mL in cup-sized bags and 24 mg for loose leaf under those conditions, compared with 200 or 400 mg daily isolated caffeine in the clinical trial. Measured constituent bridge, with no symptom observations.
Some LRRK2 groups had favorable MDS-UPDRS II composite comparisons. The idiopathic comparison was inconclusive and a separate rest-tremor estimate was unavailable.

The 26-week executive mean nominally favors high-oleic sunflower oil against either fish-oil dose, with an inconclusive difference and different 13-week ordering. Attention changes favor the active comparators. No oil-free arm, confirmed cold pressing, or Parkinson cohort.

Exploratory switching at six months was 81.1 s versus 110.1 s on coconut oil (p=.037); the within-sunflower comparison was p=.07. The supplier specification is physically refined, with no historical lot certificate. Parkinson was excluded; 31 randomized, endpoint denominator and transfer remain limited.

Refined sunflower switching moved from 130 to 131 seconds with an inconclusive arm difference. Trail Making total errors went from 1.7 to 2.5 versus 2.7 to 1.8 on MCT (adjusted p=.017). OC5 describes this same MCI family. No cold-pressed or oil-free comparison.

Relative to high-oleic sunflower, DHA shortened the composite working-memory response time by 0.36 SD (95% CI 0.14 to 0.58). This shows the relative assigned diets, with an uncertain preparation and no oral sunflower-only or Parkinson estimate.
High-oleic sunflower capsules served as active comparator for conjugated linoleic acid. Trail Making and Serial Sevens yielded no clear between-arm change. No cold pressing or Parkinson cohort.

An acute high-oleic sunflower meal produced better discrimination than a high-saturated-fat meal (p=.02). A single-meal attention comparison and multiple changing fats do not identify chronic executive impairment or an oil-alone intervention.
Sunflower frequency corresponded to +2 total PRO-PD points per frequency level (95% CI −10 to 13). A cross-sectional composite assessment did not isolate the executive symptom or pressing grade.

Images, numbers and words were recalled better after 29 days. The single-cohort before-and-after format does not control for practice and the accessible abstract lacks dosing mass, pressing grade or a distinct executive task.

Oral sunflower seed oil improved novel-object discrimination at both doses versus water in scopolamine-treated mice, both p<.001. The preparation is unverified and the model tests recognition memory without a Parkinson mechanism or executive task.

Both high-fat arms had poorer chronic spatial maze performance. A standard chow contrast changes dietary fat and energy, and there is no conventional-fat sunflower group or Parkinson disease pathology. The oil processing is unverified.

Figure 2 shows sunflower and chow near overlapping. The omnibus result and saturated-arm caption cannot assign a signed sunflower contrast. Author overlap with the original ECO member and later high-fat work leaves the experiment lineage open.

The progressive dopaminergic-loss experiment tests behavior after common tamoxifen injection in sunflower oil. There is no edible exposure contrast or separate executive measure. The later gene-expression report uses the same model but a different schedule.
Rotenone in carrier was contrasted with carrier. The difference in social recognition is a toxin-model observation; injection, common oil and different task prevent sunflower attribution.

The combined saline plus oral oil vehicle made more working-memory errors at 72 hours than untreated controls (p=.0127). Additional reference-memory errors occurred at 72 and 96 hours. The handling and saline schedule, no pressing grade and the non-Parkinson control comparison leave no transferable sign.
The reported culinary oil use has no measured neurologic outcome. Separate medicinal or ceremonial uses of the plant are contextual and do not supply an independent oil effect.
Modeled ALSFRS-R decline was 4.91 in the oil arm and 3.00 on RT001, with relative difference 1.90 (95% CI −1.39 to 5.19). The overall ALS score does not establish its swallowing item's direction.

The reflux total rose 0.33 (95% CI −2.4 to 3.1) in 18 safflower completers. Alternate allocation, shared vocal training and aggregate reflux reporting limit the inference. No separately reported swallowing item.
The earlier independent singer cohort averaged a 1-point reflux-total decline in seven safflower completers, with interaction p=.509. The separate swallowing item was unreported.

The six-month blinded safflower comparison reports caudate measurements and motor totals. The European results and two trial updates summarize this same trial family. No separate swallowing or grade verification.
Safflower and triheptanoin crossed over for Glut1 episodic movement counts. Neither swallowing nor a verifiable cold-pressed grade was reported.
The estimated swallowing safety difference favored maximum triheptanoin (−0.9, 95% CI −1.6 to −0.3) relative to MCT or periods without treatment. The study did not assign safflower.

The safflower-and-carnauba wax formulation had smoother texture. The panel spat out samples. Attendance ranged from 6 to 12 per session, with no unique participant count or swallowed test for the formulation.
The safflower-fed amyloid group showed an inflammatory gene response. Swallowing was unmeasured. Sample and overlap with the same lab's other reports require full methods.
A cold-pressed safflower diet supplies an exact processing match, in an aged mouse immune comparison. It supplies no swallowing measure. Total cohort size not established from this extract.
People swallowed capsules, and subsequent blood draws measured triglycerides. The test was designed to bypass or vary exposure to oral fat sensation, without a swallowing assessment.
This distinct protocol used two swallowed safflower capsule loads. Lipids were measured. Cohort overlap with the investigator's prior study remains unclear.
Table 2 reports oral safflower seed-oil use for other conditions. It supplies no dysphagia report and no number of participants reporting this individual plant use.
A safflower crossover measured lipids and inflammatory markers. Those endpoints supply no swallowing direction. This is the registered lipid cohort already in the assessment ledger.
Safflower in yoghurt was the control for total allergy symptom and lung measures. No isolated throat event or clinical swallowing effect was reported.

The original Fig. 1 on timed apparatus falls favors strawberry over blueberry in the wide plank and blueberry over strawberry on the rod. Fig. 1 shares letters for strawberry and unsupplemented control in all three tests. The entry cohort was 42, with five pre-completion losses. No raw fruit or spontaneous Parkinson falls.

The author reports improved spatial retention in the strawberry extract arm after irradiation. The measured result is maze learning. Same-dose pathway studies share authors and design elements, with unresolved cohort independence.

Aberdeen community study identifies severe gait abnormality in 84 of 214 clinically assessed people. Separate repeated falls and strawberry exposure are unreported. The index is a locator to this report.

Fig. 2E marks lower five-minute provoked fall count with high-dose procyanidin B2 versus the experimental injury control (4.8 versus 9.1, p<.01). The low-dose count is unmarked. The paired Fig. 2D latency plot conflicts with the prose assignment of the comparator mean. Purified reagent, cuprizone model and repeated apparatus falls do not supply a raw strawberry or Parkinson estimate.

The single-group extension reports a Fall event in two of 21 Rett participants. The registry includes strawberry flavoring as an excipient. The collection window starts in the prior randomized phase, and counts people with an event. No strawberry comparison or recurrence counts are provided.

One serious fall in each of the selected corn-oil-only placebo and fish-oil-only groups (1/71 and 1/109). These sparse counts cover serious events. The journal pooled placebo row also includes a cellulose comparator.
33/164 in pooled corn-or-soy placebo versus 42/238 on DHA, p=.60. Oil-specific allocation is unknown, recurrent outcomes are absent and population has Alzheimer dementia.

The corn-oil arm was slower on the Timed Up and Go relative to fish oil in the six-month comparison. The timed mobility task does not count falls. A fish oil benefit could explain the relative contrast.
Gait and single-leg balance comparisons are imprecise. The parent and secondary reports share both a mixed-oil control and the same participants. No fall-frequency result.
Equal-parts soybean and corn oil capsules accompanied maltodextrin. Gait and balance tasks are named. No reported fall-frequency estimate in accessible abstract and supplement.
The Parkinson comparison shares a corn-oil carrier and reports aggregate mobility. It does not isolate oil or give prospective falls.
Corn oil is shared as a vehicle in a different model. Genotype-related beam slips differ from clinical fall frequency.
Full paper and poster share solvent, animals of the same sex and strain, dosing structure and authors. Animal overlap remains uncertain and there is no falls endpoint.
The 2016 corn-oil vehicle paper and 2012 Jafari strain study have different tissues and possibly shared animals. None evaluates a fall outcome.
The perimenopause model uses injected corn oil as a vehicle and does not report falls.
Collected pharmacology members use corn oil in lipid and carrier contexts and supply no relevant fall result. Animal independence cannot be assigned from this combined locator.
The corn-oil formulation contributes to rat adiposity and lipid contrasts. The companion linkage and fall endpoint are unavailable.

Oil quantity and same symptom are separately measured. Adjusted −1.86 points (95% CI −3.54 to −0.18) with nominal p=.031. The unadjusted q=.084, main-cooking-fat comparison and unspecified grade limit transport.
The small inverse tile has no numerical estimate, uncertainty, preparation grade or adjustment. Duplicate plots belong to one cohort.

129 analyzed at baseline after exclusions and 113 completed. Each active arm reported within-group improvement. The critique describes post-treatment anxiety prevalence favoring diet alone. The adjusted oil effect and authors' response are unresolved.
Anxiety interaction p=.745 for the whole diet. Olive oil is part of that diet, with no separate intervention or verified grade.
Adjusted OR .88 (95% CI .76–.99) per point concerns the full dietary score. There is no anxiety coefficient for a separate olive-oil item.

Two verified cold-pressed oils. The higher-phenol group spent longer in open arms than water, with inconclusive center time and higher-versus-lower oil comparisons. Rat developmental and energy differences limit transfer.
Three oral groups. The abstract reports no statistically clear difference in open-field behavior and provides no group estimate. It reports separate neurogenesis findings.
More open-arm time at p<.05. Figure 2 caption gives n=5 without explicit totals and differs from methods on the control composition. No exact processing grade or Parkinson model.
The figure and results report longer latency while the abstract describes reduced latency. This inconsistency blocks a stable directional interpretation.
Table 1 has FSS 28.4 to 32.1. The same-cohort dissertation median also rises. No comparator or paired variance. Exposure and symptom are directly measured.
Seventy-seven of 80 randomized. Lower fatigue days 3–6, repeated comparison p<.001. Acute postoperative fatigue has a different trajectory than Parkinson symptom fatigue.
Reverse directional baseline heatmap for tea and fatigue. Brewing, numerical coefficient and uncertainty unavailable.
Combined sleep and fatigue domain did not show a statistically clear difference after correction. Preparations and separate fatigue outcome are unresolved.
Fatigue OR .94 (95% CI .37–2.35). Aggregate caffeine is not separately quantified brewed green tea.
Physical fatigue favored the mixture and general fatigue was inconclusive. The insomnia crossover combined tea extract, chicory and collagen.
Polyphenol intervention and composite motor endpoints. The registry has no separate Parkinson fatigue result.
Climbing and locomotor activity are animal motor outcomes. Traditional fatigue use occurs in the introduction. Complete figures and preprint body remain unverified.

Orally consumed whole ground dried Sargol powder in a study tablet versus matching placebo. Adjusted DASS difference −4.58 (95% CI −8.34 to −0.81), a registered secondary endpoint. Food quantity and other grades were not tested.
Registered Hamilton scale interaction favors saffron (p=.006). Geriatric Depression Scale and MDS-UPDRS depressed mood item were inconclusive. Capsule preparation and arm tables remain open.
2018 ground-stigma adjunct report gives intergroup BDI p=.056 with 20 per arm. Published details differ across linked reports. One family outside Parkinson disease.
Favorable Hamilton depression comparison used ethanol-extracted dried stigma rather than ground powder and excluded a defined Parkinson population.
Isolated crocin and a forced-swim phenotype in a Parkinson mouse model. Behavioral group estimates and the body remain open.
Compound and herb arms are combined interventions. Current registry has no posted result.

Adjusted Parkinson fatigue difference −9.20 (95% CI −13.76 to −4.65). The powder retains the dried edible tissue, delivered in a tablet. The standalone scale first appears in a public registry revision after outcomes manuscript receipt.
COPD-specific fatigue trajectory favored dry saffron extract. Groups began with different fatigue means. No ordinary dried stigma or Parkinson measure.
Author-reported within-group decline from a mean of 71.10 on a described scale with untransformed maximum 63. Units unclear and no control group.
Fatigue interaction p=.66. Placebo improved slightly more numerically and no interval was provided. The product and low-mood non-Parkinson population differ.
The endpoint fatigue difference favored saffron mixed with rose water and sugar. Combined intervention and independent multiple sclerosis population.
The index of slowing across sprints did not clearly differ (p=.425). It uses an acute extract and a distinct trained population and outcome.
Exploratory fatigue comparison favored extract plus sleep counseling over counseling. No matched placebo or Parkinson participants.

Whole dried Zahedi dates were fed in one of four groups of six. Hot-plate latency was shorter from month one to month two in the date arm, with no clear date-versus-chow or within-arm difference. Evoked thermal latency remains a remote Parkinson pain outcome.

After each period the abdominal-pain values were 0.22 versus 0.25. No clear difference or paired interval was reported. Masking differed between the publication and registry, with healthy participants and a low-symptom abdominal diary.

Evoked writhing and hot-plate tests favored the three ethanol extracts. They also reduced movement and prolonged drug-induced sleep. Assays have five per group and do not measure whole fruit or Parkinson pain.

The warm-surface response favored fresh date extract and the tail-flick endpoint was inconclusive. The report disagrees about significance and route details. The disease model and preparation differ from the claim.
Original author results include symptom timing without a transferable between-group cramp-severity estimate. Related articles may draw on the same people.
A multicomponent bar assigns shared date paste and the planned total includes a pain item. The separate listed item targets constipation, with no pain result posted.
The single-arm pilot reports aggregate and gastrointestinal findings. The original bar's date content and pain-item effect remain unverified.
The modern survey counts immune-support reports. Historical headache use is cited independently of its participants and no outcome is observed.

The original abstract gives an inconclusive nine-hole peg comparison without a signed estimate. The abstract reports 205 randomized and the registry lists 200 enrolled. The tested children, cooking method and motor outcome limit transfer.

The abstract lists 160 infant arm members and gives no clear Bayley psychomotor contrast. The companion biomarker report verifies salmon-containing jars in the fish arm. Numerical outcome tables remain open.
The mouse locomotion comparison favors the isolated roe fraction. It provides no bridge from the fraction to food flesh and no separately assessed Parkinson bradykinesia.

The MVP baseline program relies on participant-reported diagnosis. A small inverse graphical sign links pooled non-fried fish and self-rated slowness. This figure gives no species, grilling, separate clinical bradykinesia assessment, pair-specific estimate or interval.
The registry gives 14 enrolled after hip fracture, an assigned mixed-fish menu and termination for low recruitment. No mobility results or isolated salmon estimates are posted.

Parkinson participants took capsules of dried common-sage leaf. The actual comparator was vitamin E. The report mentions cognition and salivation but contains no apathy scale or named apathy analysis. A secondary assessment timetable was absent.

Healthy adults compared dried common-sage leaf capsules and placebo. At the higher dose, pre-task alertness favored sage at one hour while the during-task change at one hour favored placebo. Neither short-term scale contrast measures clinical apathy or its persistence.

A mixed common-sage extract and Spanish-sage essential oil comparison gave no clear mood contrast. The registered and reported trials closely match, with no explicit identifier link. They are one probable family, and clinical apathy was not measured.

The authors linked increased activity in one dose group to motivation, while other doses did not show the activity increase. The available abstract and preview give no independent apathy measure or oral dried-leaf comparison. Original tables remain open.

A purified oral constituent reduced hyperlocomotion associated with an experimental model. This direction concerns excess movement and does not measure apathy or replicate the injected-rat motivation interpretation. The complete results tables remain open.

Participants with Parkinson disease had a baseline Apathy Evaluation Scale measurement and completed an effort-choice task. Supplementary Table 2 concerns a task interaction. No sage comparison or change in clinical apathy was assessed.
Reported changes in composite cognition from a sage extract do not yield an apathy estimate or establish a dried-leaf effect in Parkinson disease.
The registry specifies cognition and stress endpoints and provides no posted clinical apathy result.
Computerized cognition and physical performance are planned in middle-aged adults. The record has no Parkinson apathy result.

Freeze-dried powder is made from whole Tifblue and Rubel berries and was compared with matched placebo. Table 2 estimates -0.3 points on the constipation item, with 95% CI -0.7 to 0.2. Food identity and the measured bowel symptom support a minimal bridge. Processing, serving context, imprecision and the non-Parkinson population limit the direction.

Two participants reported constipation during blueberry powder use. One report resolved after a pause and the other resolved spontaneously. The uncontrolled safety outcome and a non-Parkinson population give a contrary observation without an isolated severity estimate.

One possibly related constipation event occurred among 15 assigned blueberry powder and none among 14 controls. The pilot was not a constipation-severity or Parkinson trial. The journal and registry are one study family.

One mild constipation event among 106 active participants and two among 100 placebo participants. This sparse safety count is from purified bilberry and black currant, with no raw blueberry or Parkinson constipation measure. Protocol and secondary publications share this family.

No adverse events were listed in the acute whole-blueberry pharmacokinetic crossover, with 18 at risk in each condition. This duration and reporting cannot substitute for longitudinal constipation severity in Parkinson disease.
The cohort of 61 completers had symptoms collected from caregivers, but no separate constipation outcome was reported. The microbiome and clinical reports share this cohort.
The Parkinson trial uses wild blueberry powder and registers motor outcomes. No constipation severity outcome or comparative results were available.
The direction for pooled fresh fruit uses a constructed constipation category, with missing or nondaily bowel reports and no blueberry-specific estimate. It cannot isolate the frozen food.
A pooled berry item in the dietary study had a lower total Parkinson symptom score. The constipation comparison concerns overall dietary scores and supplies no separate raw-blueberry estimate.
The study measures bowel diaries but blueberries are one part of a shared mixed meal. There is no isolated blueberry estimate.

Some participants reported more constipation during a blueberry and grape seed extract adjunct. Neither exact counts nor isolation of blueberry from other ingredients and concurrent treatment is verified in the original abstract.
The live and sterilized preparations combine processing and fermentation differences. Stool-form changes do not establish a raw-blueberry constipation effect, and chronic constipation was excluded.

New drooling occurred immediately while the child had oral and facial swelling and other symptoms of a likely allergic reaction. Positive allergy testing corroborates the exposure history. No oral challenge or Parkinson saliva or swallowing outcome was available. Acute allergy supplies no directional estimate for changes in chronic Parkinson drooling.

Both active syrup groups report more drooling events than placebo, with 17/40 versus 15/40 between active arms. Neither raw fig nor a matched addition of fig was assigned. The child ADHD population and lack of drooling grades leave no transferable efficacy sign.
Drooling and dysphagia were observed in secondary parkinsonism. The reported medication response concerns other symptoms. The case gives no paired dietary and salivary comparison.
Two continuing apomorphine users described less drooling after stimulation. No raw-fig comparison or graded drooling outcome was reported.

Paper-filtered regular coffee reduced acute mental fatigue versus flavored water in a randomized crossover (adjusted p=.01). Beverage preparation and reported outcome family fit. The healthy habitual-use and abstention setting, brief assessment and partially successful masking limit transfer.

Table 2 reports caffeine-versus-placebo FSS change differences of -3.08 and -2.85 at weeks three and six. Both credible intervals span zero. Caffeine is a separately measured component of the matched filtered coffee, with no assumption of equal doses or effect sizes. This reaches clinical fatigue but adds only a minimal constituent bridge.

Three individual mean fatigue contrasts favored regular espresso and one went in the opposite direction. No pooled estimate. Both arms used brewed espresso and washouts substituted decaf. Caffeine level, withdrawal and within-person differences matter. A population-level sign for consumption versus no coffee is unavailable.

Unfiltered coffee versus water had no reported fatigue interaction. Raw late fatigue means favored water, while the text described a mitigating trend. This early healthy adult comparison limits extension of the filtering result across brew types.
Soluble caffeinated coffee gave a lower acute mental fatigue change than regular decaf or flavored placebo. Industrial soluble preparation and a healthy sample limit use to corroborating context.
Pre-to-post tiredness change favored breakfast. Both assigned croissants were paired with espresso. There is no coffee-free or time control and no tested coffee effect.
Reported overall caffeine frequency yielded fatigue OR 0.94 (95% CI 0.37 to 2.35). This highly uncertain observational grouping does not provide a sign for brewed coffee.
The longer capsule trial planned an individual fatigue item. No posted results or separate reported fatigue contrast was recovered. Daytime somnolence is a different item.
The diabetes and restless legs study lists coffee cups and FSS in separate tables without an exposure-specific estimate or a Parkinson group.

Standardized oral extract derived from the stigma contains documented crocin isomers and safranal. Primary ISI change interaction p=.017 versus matched oral placebo. Parkinson disease was excluded. Self-report, attrition and supplier funding limit transfer.

Pooled adjusted AIS difference −0.95 points (95% CI −1.79 to −0.11). The day-28 comparison spans 150 participants and 158 have baseline data in the reported ITT cohort. The dose-specific contrasts did not resolve independently. The oral stigma extract and whole powder differ. Preprint and final paper are one family.

A separate registration and cohort. The abstract reports favorable secondary ISQ totals and classifications; arm estimates and analysis denominators remain unverified. The registry and paper are one family.

Same Parkinson cohort and ground Sargol stigma in a tablet. An overall sleep-quality contrast favors saffron. A separate insomnia-severity estimate was not reported in the accessible original outcomes.
The older-adult randomized trial has an inconclusive ISI interaction (p=.3). Results on other sleep measures cannot substitute for an insomnia contrast.

Three insomnia adverse events in each group. Depression was the efficacy outcome. The extract is from flower petals, fluoxetine is an active comparator and overlap with the other Tehran petal study is unverified.

Preprint Table 3 reports an inconclusive global PSQI interaction (p=.2) and latency interaction (p=.7). Two secondary components favor extract in ITT and do not resolve per protocol. Registry and preprint belong to one trial.
PROMIS sleep disturbance contrast 0.38 points (95% CI −2.40 to 3.16). A separate sleep-related impairment result favors extract. Neither is an isolated insomnia severity estimate.
Abstract reports that both arms improved on ISI. It provides no between-arm ISI difference. Route and mixed botanicals prevent assigning the result to oral ground saffron.
The prospective extract study identifies ISI as secondary. Recruiting record has no posted results and does not study culinary powder or a Parkinson cohort.

Fifteen each received powder, placebo and a separate yeast arm. Day-20 constipation severity was 49.13 versus 65.86 for ginger and placebo, with baseline imbalance and a crude change difference of −11.79 points. The reported table threshold concerns arm comparisons, and the crude contrast has no adjusted uncertainty. The same rhizome and same symptom permit minimal transfer across preparation and population.

The ginger capsule group began higher and ended at 1.09 versus 1.80 on the constipation domain, p=.016. The adjusted result applies to a separate overall score. Registry and paper identify one trial. The same symptom and rhizome permit a minimal link, with no direct dietary Parkinson result.

The adjusted constipation-severity changes were −24.15 and +11.39 on a 100 mm scale. Gingerol-standardized tablets and relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis limit exposure and population transfer. The older clinical outcomes paper and newer review repeat the same trial family.

The pulverized-rhizome group went from 1.06 to 0.38 on the constipation item and placebo from 0.98 to 1.04, reported p<.001 at end. A treated thyroid cohort and a capsule preparation limit transfer to the culinary Parkinson question.
PAC-SYM and stool frequency favored the extract in 55 completers, while stool consistency was inconclusive. Funding, attrition imbalances and inconsistent extract amounts limit extrapolation.

Among adults with functional dyspepsia, the registered ginger extract trial reported a 2.9-point difference in constipation score changes, with 80 randomized. Steaming, extraction and diagnostic setting limit transfer.

Composite IBS responders were numerically more frequent with placebo and there was no clear group difference. Difficulty passing stool was reported without arm-specific counts. The trial gives no separate efficacy estimate for constipation.

One constipation adverse event was reported with extract versus zero listed on placebo. The small event count and unset severity leave a safety lead, with no interpretable change in the frozen symptom.

Six Parkinson patients reported easier defecation and faster mean colonic transit under a shared formula. Ginger, ginseng and pepper were assigned together, and efficacy significance was pooled with multiple system atrophy observations.
Secondary first defecation was around six hours earlier with ginger after cesarean delivery. Long-term symptom severity outside surgery was unmeasured. Trial and registration are one source family.
Ginger capsules versus placebo yielded a 12.6-hour earlier secondary first stool after surgery. The comparison uses perioperative recovery and does not assess a chronic symptom.
Ileus occurred in 23 patients per arm and time to first flatus was similar. Stool timing was incomplete. Enhanced recovery alone was the comparator and the outcome differs from chronic constipation.
The trial compares two capsule strengths and prioritizes ghrelin. Gut transit and GI symptoms are listed as other outcomes. Recruitment is active and there are no reported results.

The public bilingual record compares standardized powder tablets with placebo. It prioritizes total MDS-UPDRS and gives no separate constipation outcome. Recruitment is listed complete and results remain unavailable.

Applied gingerol suppressed spontaneous contraction in isolated rat distal-colon longitudinal muscle. This is a lower-motility observation under laboratory conditions without a stool or severity measurement or evidence of exposure at the same concentrations after eating ginger.

A participant reports regular bowel movements with a smoothie containing ginger and other ingredients and reports using cereal as an alternative. Dose, the role of ginger and the contributor's diagnosis are unresolved.
A person reporting IBS-C describes less stomach pain with tea and chews and no clearly perceived constipation relief. No comparative symptom measure or verified exposure composition.
A public report describes no stool during two weeks after switching from a helpful aloe preparation to ginger. Pre-existing constipation and stopping aloe prevent separating effects.

Separate replies describe bowel regularity while taking powdered capsules and later worsening after illness with unspecified ginger. The source links a cross-post and the known gingerol experiment. No independent diagnosis or comparable exposure.

Double-blind RCT of 2 tbsp/day raw extra-virgin versus refined olive oil for 4 weeks in adults with chronic constipation; Rome III adjusted difference -4.22 (printed 95% CI 3.63-4.82, p < 0.001) and week-4 BSFS +1.14 (95% CI 0.94-1.35, p < 0.001). Per-protocol after 5 taste/odor withdrawals per arm, no oil-free arm, no polyphenol assay, printed week-1 table typo, and neurological causes excluded. Same trial as IRCT20080901001155N33.

Author abstract of ulcerative colitis crossover (40 enrolled, 32 completers) reports reduced GSRS constipation after 20 days of extra-virgin olive oil (p < 0.05). Full text and between-oil contrast versus canola oil remain paywalled, keeping this family contextual.

Four-week hemodialysis trial compared unspecified olive oil (10.3 to 3.2) with mineral oil (10.5 to 4.1) and flaxseed oil (9.6 to 6.0); group-by-time p = 0.15 across active comparators, grade unspecified and non-Parkinson population.

Parkinson Mediterranean diet plus standard care versus standard care alone (45 randomized, 36 analyzed); median GSRS constipation change -0.5 vs -0.8 (p = 0.600) with no isolated olive-oil arm or specified grade.

Uncontrolled five-week Parkinson Mediterranean diet pilot; mean GSRS constipation fell from 2.25 to 1.54 (p = 0.04) alongside increased fiber (24.8 to 36.2 g) and oleic acid, with no control arm, oil dose or grade.

Parkinson Mediterranean-ketogenic versus Mediterranean-MCT crossover encouraged olive oil in both phases with grade unspecified; bowel frequency OR 1.03 (95% CI 0.82-1.28) and MDS-UPDRS constipation unchanged in either phase.

Nursing-home RCT of topical abdominal massage with extra-virgin olive oil (5.62 to 2.06) versus water massage (5.05 to 3.11) and usual care (4.44 to 5.22), p <= 0.001; topical route with massage and non-Parkinson cohort.
Uncontrolled pediatric epilepsy ketogenic program where extra-virgin olive oil supplied 80-85% of fat recorded constipation in 102/389 (26.2%); whole ketogenic regimen and no oil-free comparator.
Cross-sectional Parkinson dietary analysis found adjusted OR 0.88 (95% CI 0.77-0.98, p = 0.035) per composite Mediterranean score point, without a separate extra-virgin olive-oil constipation model.
Registered six-month modified Mediterranean diet protocol in Parkinson disease includes raw olive oil advice and constipation endpoints, with no isolated oil arm, assigned grade or posted results.

Registered factorial Mediterranean diet and activity protocol specifies extra-virgin olive oil as main added fat and schedules GSRS constipation and Bristol stool form, with no oil-only arm or posted results.
Uncontrolled public caregiver report of softer stool after one week of olive oil shots alongside concurrent walking; initial hard stool persisted and oil grade was unspecified.
Uncontrolled public forum report of constipation resolution after adding unspecified olive oil while removing wheat and changing breakfast; simultaneous dietary changes prevent attribution.

Randomized 3-arm trial (IRCT2013122114668N2; likely overlapping PMC4443385) reports lower VAS menstrual pain for cinnamon bark powder capsules vs starch placebo at 24-72 h (ibuprofen lower). Non-Parkinson pain etiology and minor 48 h placebo discrepancy across companion reports.

Randomized 60-day trial (50 assigned, 43 completers; same cohort as 2024 PMC11210698) reports C. zeylanicum bark powder capsules lowered migraine VAS 7.61->3.33 vs 7.54->6.77 on starch (adjusted p<.001). Retrospective registration (44 vs 50) and migraine population limit transfer.

Randomized 8-week trial in women with rheumatoid arthritis reports lower VAS pain with cinnamon powder capsules vs placebo (abstract p<.001). Full numeric table and participant flow remain unavailable.

Randomized 8-week MS trial (60 assigned, 41 analyzed) reports VAS 54.28->24.76 vs 41.50->43.25 (p=.003), but severe attrition, baseline pain imbalance, unresolved macerate-vs-powder wording, and registered PQAS vs reported VAS prevent signing.
Two-cycle dysmenorrhea capsule trial abstract reports time-by-treatment p=.02 but conflicts across Results and Conclusion wording, with full text and capsule form unverified.
Oral cinnamon powder exercise-soreness trial prints inconsistent p values and durations across sections, supplying no clear easing or worsening direction.
Randomized dyspepsia trial comparing cinnamon bark oil macerate in sesame oil versus sesame oil alone found an inconclusive upper abdominal pain contrast (primary outcome was bloating).
Single Parkinson rehabilitation case had lower back pain during multimodal therapy plus a routine cassia-containing herbal prescription; cointerventions block cinnamon attribution.

Oral isolated beta-caryophyllene eased late formalin and neuropathic mechanical responses in mice but was inconclusive on early formalin and tail-flick; isolated terpene does not estimate culinary ground cinnamon.
Topical cinnamon essential-oil gel lowered late-phase formalin rat pain with inconclusive early-phase and thermal comparisons; non-oral oil preparation and rodent proxy.

Park 2026 OA15.04 (plus lifestyle protocol PMID:26976087, pediatric elimination PMC4070603, and cell blend PMC11208286) tracks culinary spice intake or blends without isolating a ground-cinnamon pain effect.

Randomized thyroid-biopsy trial (52 commercial 90% vanilla-flavored dark chocolate 20 g vs 47 no snack) reports STAI 39.79->34.31 vs 38.60->38.89 (group-by-time p=.01, d=.48). Unblinded without matched snack and acute procedural non-Parkinson anxiety.

Three-day open-label randomized comparison in nursing students reports lower HADS (5 vs 7, p=.001) and DASS (10 vs 16, p<.001) anxiety with dark chocolate vs mineral water; unblinded unmatched comparator and minor range inconsistencies.

Parallel snack comparison (74% dark chocolate vs two control snacks) found no statistically clear state-anxiety change in habitual anxiety strata (Results 3.2), serving as a key competing null result.

Masked 8-week 85% cocoa vs simulated chocolate crossover in severe CFS reports within-period HADS changes (9.5->6 p=.01 vs 6->9 p=.03) with a 3.5-point baseline mismatch and no between-treatment contrast.

Double-blind brewed-cocoa crossover (NCT01651793) found no cocoa-vs-water mood interaction; task anxiety favored caffeinated cocoa vs caffeine alone (p=.038). Beverage form and mental stress task differ from plain solid chocolate.

Mediterranean diet counseling in Parkinson disease limited dark chocolate to <=1 serving/week and showed an inconclusive HAM-A anxiety interaction (p=.745); whole-diet design cannot isolate dark chocolate.
Parkinson case-control study observed higher chocolate craving in PD and higher anxiety in a pooled food-addiction subgroup without estimating a dark-chocolate intake effect on PD anxiety.

FlaSeCo compared high- vs low-flavanol dark chocolate on depression/cognition without isolated anxiety results; rotenone rat study (PMC12227552) and Crete stress registry (ISRCTN11805689) report no anxiety severity outcome.

Two randomized 11-day trials in healthy volunteers (34 raw ground ginger, 40 heat-treated ground ginger capsules vs placebo) report lower 24-hour eccentric-exercise muscle pain. Encapsulated ground rhizome and induced soreness differ from grated ginger in Parkinson pain.
Randomized placebo-controlled trial reports lower menstrual VAS pain with ginger root powder capsules under two dosing schedules; abstract-only verification and primary dysmenorrhea population.

Randomized acute-migraine trial reports more 2-hour pain-free responders with standardized ginger extract plus ketoprofen versus placebo plus ketoprofen (56.7% vs 33.3%, p=.03). Extract add-on and acute headache differ from grated ginger in PD.

Placebo-controlled steamed ginger extract (GGE03) trial in functional dyspepsia reports GSRS abdominal pain change -5.0 vs -1.2 (p<.001) and favorable SF-36 bodily pain (same cohort as constipation report).
Publisher abstract reports favorable VAS and K-WOMAC knee osteoarthritis pain for steamed ginger extract GGE03 vs placebo; full numeric arm tables and registration remain open.
Blinded 8-week powdered ginger versus placebo trial in knee osteoarthritis found no clear KOOS pain advantage, supplying a direct competing null trial for oral rhizome powder.
Ninety-day randomized migraine-prevention trial of standardized ginger extract found inconclusive >=50% response (42% vs 39%) and severe-pain days versus placebo.
Supercritical ginger extract trial during exercise testing found an inconclusive multivariate WOMAC pain group-by-time interaction (p=.690); retrospective registration.
Randomized hysterectomy enhanced-recovery trial showed no clear difference in postoperative or epigastric pain scores for ginger capsules versus placebo.

Competing null or methodologically conflicted non-PD trials: Black 2010 acute crossover (n=27 null), Bliddal 2000 OA crossover (unclear overall), Shirvani 2015 vs mefenamic acid (no placebo), Wu 2008/2011 GI symptoms (null), TCTR20220124002 craniotomy (null), plus quasi-experiments and reporting discrepancies (DOI10.1055/s-0039-1700705, JRNM.2013.068, PMID42765050, PMID42829743).
Active UK recruiting Ginger-PD trial (n=72 PD/RBD/controls, ginger extract capsules 12 weeks) targets ghrelin and inflammatory/gut biomarkers rather than pain severity, with no posted results.

Brasilia PD thesis names ginger among foods said to relieve body aches without preparation or counts; Shiota PD case used multi-herb Dai-Kenchu-To; mixed formulas (Herbagut, Rikkunshito, ginger-artichoke, ginger-galangal) and animal/traditional accounts cannot isolate grated ginger.

Unblinded primary-dysmenorrhea trial adding oral whole turmeric powder to naproxen reports VAS decrease 7.0 vs 5.6 (p<.001), but conflicts with linked registry NCT04183556 (90 actual crossover vs 149 parallel) and prints an implausible Table 1 SD.

Double-blind pilot of 3 g/day whole turmeric powder capsules vs placebo in hand osteoarthritis found inconclusive primary 1-month and between-group pain contrasts at all visits; 3-month p=.032/.017 are within-arm vs baseline with baseline imbalance.

Formulated Turmipure Gold trial (NCT04946981, n=44) had inconclusive primary 72 h soreness AUC; standardized curcumin extract in digestive complaints (DOI10.1186/s12906-021-03220-6) gave unclear SF-36 pain contrast; BCM-95 RA trial (PMID22407780) lacked placebo.

Ground turmeric chronic-pain crossover (PMID41599836, n=29) gave turmeric to both arms to test black pepper addition (p=.157); Mediterranean-diet pilot (PMID37521415), Herbagut (PMID29554961), and ZAZ2 (PMID21687764) did not isolate ground turmeric.

Oral, intrathecal, and injected isolated curcumin (PMID16584726, PMID29339457, PMID32171311) and combined ginger-turmeric extract (PMID32839804) reduced evoked rodent nociception without testing whole ground turmeric or Parkinson pain.

PD supplement survey (PMID36839160 pooled composite), PRIME-NL exposure survey (PMID38943398), Brasilia interview (ambiguous acafrao term), herbalist survey (tel-03267487), and Barbados/Mekong traditional surveys give no isolated ground-turmeric pain estimate.

Double-blind menopause trial of fresh Salvia officinalis tip extract tablets vs placebo (80 randomized, 78 ITT, 48 per-protocol) reports favorable MRS joint and muscular discomfort change (p<.05); exact item effect size and ITT item estimate unreported.

Placebo-controlled 12-week trial (66 assigned, 59 analyzed; IRCT2015111713940N2) reports lower MRS joint and muscular discomfort with dry sage extract vs placebo (p<.001), with reversed table mean/SD printing limiting exact magnitude.
Randomized phase-two trial reports 2-hour throat-pain AUC favored 15% vs 0.3% common sage leaf extract spray (p=.0021); topical local route and acute pharyngitis differ from oral fresh sage in PD.
Single non-Parkinson case reports 6/10 abdominal pain after excessive common-sage plant intake of unknown preparation/dose; coexisting symptoms and concurrent treatments leave causation uncertain.

Dried sage leaf extract Alzheimer trial reports 2 vs 0 abdominal pain adverse events (p=.23) with section count discrepancies; adverse-event count does not measure pain severity or culinary fresh sage.

OralHAC cancer rinse omitted sparse pain items; active-controlled postoperative/mucositis/cold-sore trials (PMID24672091, PMID22875590, PMID11799306), inhaled labor/cesarean aromas, mixed-herb protocols (NCT00707902, NCT04038749, NCT04054284, NCT06889961, PMC10664317), and pooled Wightman events give no isolated oral fresh-sage pain estimate.

Oral/injected Salvia officinalis extracts reduced evoked mechanical/thermal/formalin nociception in rodents (PMID31341489, PMID22154965, PMID20860437, DOI10.3724/sp.j.1009.2011.00354) and high-dose toxicity tail-prick (PMC11949616); preclinical proxies only.
Randomized stable-angina trial of powdered lemon-balm leaf capsules vs placebo reports favorable adjusted depression contrast, though baseline symptoms were low and adjusted CI was unreported.

Randomized type 2 diabetes trial (60 assigned, 44 completers) reports BDI-II change -3.91 vs -0.04 for lemon-balm extract capsules vs placebo (adjusted p=.001), with higher extract baseline and trial-length wording discrepancy.
Randomized trial of formulated phospholipid lemon-balm extract vs placebo in adults with emotional distress/poor sleep reports favorable DASS-42 group-by-time depression contrast.
Postpartum capsule trial reports smaller day-14 EPDS rise under lemon balm (+1.9 vs +6.2, p=.004); both arms rose from low baselines and attrition/table denominators are unresolved.
Randomized active-comparator trial adding dried-leaf lemon balm to egg isolate found no clear difference on HAM-D (8.4 vs 10.1) or BDI-II (11.0 vs 10.5), supplying a key competing null result.

Retrospectively registered burn-injury trial comparing brewed Melissa vs black tea shows favorable marginals, but Table 3 p=.002 is within-arm, Table 5 differences are undefined, and early discharges were replaced.
Aqueous leaf extract trial had severe-depression counts 3/28->3/28 vs 10/27->6/27 with baseline imbalance and no verified between-group change.

Adolescent PMS family (PMID29369810, IRCT2014060717998N1, PMID26339667) and CABG HADS report (IRCT2014071918531N1) have unreconciled test statistics, missing baselines, or overlapping cohort ambiguity.

Includes pooled PD survey (ECBN260617), Serbian/Wroclaw surveys, dialysis inhalation null (PMID40082838 p=.84), acute calmness Lemcog null (PMID41782777), multi-herb blends (Nepeta, IBS, STW5, Ze185), pending brewed-tea registries (UMIN000055134, IRCT20190204042617N2, NCT05422599), and mixed rodent assays.

Randomized SSRI add-on trial of dried ground rosemary leaf capsules (51 completers) reports BDI-II group-by-time p=.005, limited by baseline imbalance (p=.003) without covariate adjustment and non-Parkinson cohort.

Dried rosemary capsule trial in university students (34/arm) describes favorable mood in its abstract, while the Aucoin poster extracts endpoint depression SMD -0.30 (95% CI -0.78 to 0.18) and full analysis remains open.
Randomized rosemary extract trial during methadone maintenance found no significant HADS depression difference (exact means/CIs omitted; dose/duration wording conflicts).
Rosemary extract trial in Japanese working men (UMIN000036762) found an inconclusive post hoc depression comparison (p=.058).
Same-team 2026 review/poster family pools five depression comparisons at SMD -0.29 (95% CI -1.01 to 0.42, I2=85%) using end scores across mismatched baselines; context-only synthesis.

Fresh-derived rosemary water trials (PMID30318972, neurosci7010015, aces.2018.83013) omit clinical depression; botanical blend (PMID38887495 BDI-II p=.149), shared-arm NCT01178892, odor/massage trials, and rodent assays give no isolated fresh-leaf depression effect.

Randomized depression trial adding nigella oil extract to sertraline vs sertraline alone reports DASS-21 endpoint means 18.6 vs 23.4 (p<.001), with a one-point discrepancy between printed change and means; oil co-treatment outside PD.
Ground nigella seed capsule trial favored a post-treatment premenstrual composite mood domain rather than depression severity; depression inventory was used for screening only.
Crushed nigella seed capsule placebo comparison showed no clear between-arm Bond-Lader mood difference.

Combined nigella-ajwain-lime in hypothyroidism (PMID39086868, BDI-II p=.79) and nigella-flax in MS (IRCT20140617018126N6, n=35) were inconclusive; hemodialysis HADS (IRCT20200411047027N1) remains unreported; rat toxin models (rotenone, manganese) are preclinical proxies.
Randomized 12-week trial (66 assigned, 59 completers) reports lower final PSQI with dry Salvia officinalis extract tablets vs placebo (mean 9.4 to 5.6) in postmenopausal women.
Double-blind Menosan trial (78 ITT postmenopausal women) reports better 4-week sleep quality and psychosomatic sleep ratings with fresh-tip extract vs placebo (MRS sleep item trend).

Dormitory trial (64/arm, room allocation; IRCT20141125020082N2) reports lower 1-month PSQI for 10 g sage + 3 g sugar tea vs 13 g brown sugar (9.93->8.21 vs 9.89->10.60, p=.00); unequal sugar, missing responder counts, and baseline typo limit reliability.

Active-controlled primary-insomnia pilot (15 dried sage tea vs 15 chamomile) reports inconclusive day-14 and day-21 ISI contrasts (p=.78, .83) with baselines below stated eligibility and no inactive control.

Newcastle Parkinson dried-sage vs vitamin-E pilot (EudraCT 2007-002899-34) reports cognition and salivation without a sleep/insomnia estimate; prostate composite (NCT00541788), mixed-aroma trial (PMID42011111), pending registries (NCT06889961, NCT07806838), and rat sedation give no isolated dried-sage insomnia effect.
Placebo-controlled trial of proprietary nigella oil extract (BCO-5) in non-restorative sleepers reports improved PSQI and sleep components at 45 and 90 days; proprietary oil outside PD.

Separately registered 7-day double-blind placebo-controlled actigraphy trial at the same site reports improved sleep efficiency, latency, and duration with BCO-5 oil extract (corrigendum corrects placebo p value).
Postmenopausal nigella extract placebo comparison reports PSQI 7.2->6.6 vs 11->9.5 (overall p=.45) with conflicting narrative scores and unverified ground-seed identity.

Active crossover (PMID42819242) favored melatonin over nigella oil; multi-herb chronic insomnia formula (PMID41623556, p=.27) was inconclusive; nasal drops (NCT05494164) and pending oil registry (NCT06950424) give no ground-seed insomnia estimate.
Randomized menopause trial (IRCT20200104046001N1, n=60) reports 1-month insomnia scores 5.6 vs 11.0 (p<.001) favoring sweet-basil leaf extract vs placebo; extract preparation outside PD.
Independent triple-blind postpartum trial (IRCT20220926056046N2) of dried sweet-basil aerial powder vs placebo found no clear total sleep-quality difference (17.63 vs 16.15, adjusted p=.400).
Injected isolated myrcene prolonged acute pentobarbital sleep (PMID12587690) while repeated dosing shortened barbiturate sleep via drug metabolism (PMID8257941); non-culinary drug-sleep proxy.

Randomized tart-cherry concentrate trial favored treatment-mean mental fatigue by 9.5 points (95% CI 2.5 to 16.5, p=.009), with inconclusive treatment-by-repetition (p=.257); concentrate and non-PD session fatigue limit transfer.
Randomized ulcerative-colitis trial (35 completers) found inconclusive secondary IBD fatigue severity and impact differences for tart-cherry concentrate versus placebo.
Acute tart-cherry concentrate crossover (PMID27989253, n=27, p=.690) and 2-week cherry-apple juice crossover (PMID20438325, n=15) both found inconclusive fatigue comparisons.

Multiple athlete trials found null fatigue contrasts: marathon VAS (PMID41677899, n=35), sprint fatigue (PMID41683264, n=40), rugby crossover (PMID32672095, n=11), pretraining (Swinbourne 2015), cyclist muscle fatigue (PMID39141644), soccer well-being (PMID31188696), and cycling exhaustion (PMID30932750).
